items.stimulus: On a globe, two meridians of longitude meet at the North Pole. The angle between them, measured at Earth's axis, is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ radians.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of this angle?
items.explanation: To change radians to degrees, multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$: $\frac{\pi}{6} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} = \frac{180}{6} = 30$. The angle between the meridians is $30^\circ$.

A.why: You multiplied by $\frac{\pi}{180}$, which is the degrees-to-radians factor. Going from radians to degrees, you multiply by $\frac{180}{\pi}$ so that the $\pi$ cancels.

C.why: You divided 180 by 6 correctly but left $\pi$ in the answer. A degree measure has no $\pi$ in it, because $\pi$ radians is the same as $180^\circ$, so the $\pi$ should cancel.

D.why: You treated $\pi$ radians as $360^\circ$ and got $\frac{360}{6}$. A full circle is $2\pi$ radians, so $\pi$ radians is only $180^\circ$.

items.stimulus: A printmaker turns a carved block on the press bed through an angle of $\theta$ radians, where $\frac{3\theta}{4} = \frac{9\pi}{10} - \frac{\pi}{5}$.
items.stem: What is the measure, in degrees, of $\theta$?
items.explanation: Test the choices. Convert 168° to radians: $168 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{14\pi}{15}$. Then $\frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{14\pi}{15} = \frac{42\pi}{60} = \frac{7\pi}{10}$, and the right side is $\frac{9\pi}{10} - \frac{2\pi}{10} = \frac{7\pi}{10}$, so they match. Solving forward: $\theta = \frac{4}{3} \cdot \frac{7\pi}{10} = \frac{14\pi}{15}$ radians, and $\frac{14\pi}{15} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi} = 168$ degrees.

A.why: You multiplied $\frac{7\pi}{10}$ by $\frac{3}{4}$ when you needed to divide by it. That gives $\frac{21\pi}{40}$, which is 94.5°.

B.why: You converted the right side, $\frac{7\pi}{10}$, which is 126°. That's the value of $\frac{3\theta}{4}$, not of $\theta$. You still had to multiply by $\frac{4}{3}$.

D.why: You multiplied $\frac{14\pi}{15}$ by 180 but didn't divide by $\pi$, so the $\pi$ stayed in a degree answer. The factor is $\frac{180}{\pi}$, and it cancels the $\pi$.
